strengths: The task is useful and clearly motivated: retrieve a person using a reference image and a description of changed attributes. ITCPR contributes 2,202 composed queries and a 20,510-image gallery, with manual relative captions and additional checks for missing positives.

The two-stage approach is practical: adapt CLIP using existing person image-caption datasets, then train a lightweight image-to-token mapper without CPR training triplets. The overall pipeline is understandable and computationally accessible.

Reported improvements over simple fusion are substantial on both backbones. The text-supervised ViT-L/14 model achieves 45.549% Rank-1 and 55.260% mAP, versus 32.016% and 41.831% for image-text feature averaging.

The appendix provides useful experiments on loss functions, training-data volume, architecture, ensembles, and inference time. Table B supports the CMPM training choice, with approximately 3.1–3.4 percentage-point Rank-1 improvements over ITC. Many training hyperparameters and hardware details are provided.
weaknesses: The main comparison with prior composed retrieval methods is confounded. Table 1 and Section 5.2 state that Pic2Word and SEARLE reuse mappings trained with the original CLIP parameters, including when evaluated with fine-tuned encoders. Word4Per instead learns its mapping after domain adaptation. Retraining competitors with the same encoders and person data is necessary to isolate the proposed contribution. Table B partially addresses loss choice but does not resolve this central comparison problem.

The evaluation appears to use the test benchmark for model selection. Section 4 designates ITCPR exclusively for testing, while Section 5.3 selects network depth, width, template, and token length using its results. No independent CPR validation split or alternative selection protocol is reported. This materially weakens confidence in the final generalization estimates. Missing repeated runs or uncertainty estimates also make small prompt and ensemble improvements difficult to assess.

Methodological originality is limited. Mapping images into pseudo-word tokens for composed retrieval closely follows Pic2Word and SEARLE, while CLIP adaptation and identity-aware matching build on established person-retrieval methods. The task and benchmark are meaningful contributions, but the experiments do not sufficiently establish what capability arises specifically from the proposed combination.

Benchmark validation needs more detail. Appendix B.1 corrects missing positives using retrieval from an unspecified visual encoder, without reporting the retrieval cutoff or auditing remaining omissions. Annotation agreement and performance by source dataset or modification type are also absent. These gaps limit assessment of label completeness and whether pooled gains reflect robust person-specific composition.

Some details affecting interpretation and reproduction are ambiguous. Table 1 presents the combined setting as L_Vis + L_Text, whereas Appendix C.4 describes fusion of multiple TINets; joint optimization and ensembling should be distinguished explicitly. Equation 1 also includes vocabulary-size normalization whose implementation needs clarification because Equation 5 combines the losses without weights.

The proposed dataset release and explicit person-identification applications warrant documentation of source licenses, redistribution permissions, and privacy considerations. The manuscript does not address these or the surveillance misuse implications. This is a documentation concern; the manuscript does not establish that unauthorized collection occurred.
